procedural_history.impugned_order: Order dated 28th November, 2011, rejecting the appellant's petition under Section 7-A of the JJ Act, 2000, claiming to be a juvenile in conflict with law. Also, an earlier similar application by the appellant was rejected by the Chief Judicial Magistrate.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The learned Division Bench of Patna High Court heard Criminal Appeal No. 518 of 2013.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court after the Patna High Court's decision. The Supreme Court is hearing Criminal Appeal No. 177 of 2018 (and potentially related appeals Criminal Appeal No. 214 of 2018).

directions: List along with Criminal Appeal No. 177 of 2018.

issue.issue_text: Whether a challenge to a conviction can be made on the ground that the courts below failed to consider the petitioner's plea of juvenility on the date of the commission of the offence.

facts: The petitioner challenged his conviction under Sections 302 and 394 of the IPC.
The basis for the challenge was that the lower courts (both the trial court and the High Court) failed to consider his plea that he was a juvenile on the date the offence was committed.
The petitioner had specifically raised this plea in his appeal before the High Court, but the court did not address it.
law: The Supreme Court cited a consistent line of its own decisions establishing that a plea of juvenility can be raised at any stage of legal proceedings.
This includes raising the plea for the first time before the Supreme Court, even after the case has been finally disposed of.
This principle is codified in Section 9(2) of the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection) Act, 2015, which states that the plea can be raised before any court at any stage.
The Court emphasized that the objective of the JJ Act is the reformation and rehabilitation of the juvenile, and this purpose should not be defeated by a hyper-technical approach.
application: The Court found that the High Court was in error for not considering the petitioner's plea of juvenility, especially since the JJ Act, 2015 was in force at the time of the appeal.
It noted that a proper inquiry, as required by the JJ Act, was never conducted by the lower courts despite the plea being raised.
The Court concluded that a plea of juvenility, once raised, cannot be dismissed or ignored without conducting a proper inquiry to determine the person's age.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the petitioner's challenge, holding that the lower courts erred by failing to consider and conduct a proper inquiry into the plea of juvenility. The Court affirmed that such a plea can be raised at any stage and must be duly considered by the courts as per the mandate of the Juvenile Justice Act.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a challenge to a conviction can be made on the ground that the courts below failed to consider the petitioner's plea of juvenility on the date of the commission of the offence.
appellant_arguments: The trial court dismissed the plea of juvenility in a perfunctory manner without conducting a proper inquiry.
The dismissal was based solely on the ground that a similar prayer had been previously rejected by the Chief Judicial Magistrate.
respondent_arguments: The plea of juvenility was highly belated and should not be entertained by the Supreme Court.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: No hard-and-fast rule can be prescribed for the prima facie acceptance or rejection of documents submitted to prove juvenility; if such documents prima facie inspire the confidence of the court, the court may act upon them for the purposes of ordering an inquiry for the determination of age.
obiter: The Juvenile Justice Act is a beneficent and remedial legislation that aims to grant care, protection, and rehabilitation to a juvenile, promoting their well-being and applying the principle of proportionality.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: A plea of juvenility can be raised at any stage of legal proceedings, even if not taken before the trial court or the High Court, and can be raised before the Supreme Court even after the final disposal of the case. The courts must consider such a plea and should not dismiss it on hypertechnical grounds, as the Juvenile Justice Act is a beneficent and remedial legislation.
legal_tests_applied: A plea of juvenility should be considered prima facie on the touchstone of preponderance of probability.
The plea of juvenility may be raised before any Court and it shall be recognised at any stage, even after final disposal of the case.
policy_considerations: The Juvenile Justice Act is a beneficent and remedial legislation aimed at the grant of care, protection, and rehabilitation of a juvenile, and courts should be guided by its objectives to ensure its salutary provisions are not defeated by a hypertechnical approach.

The rule allowing a plea of juvenility to be raised at a considerably belated stage has its rationale in contemporary child rights jurisprudence which requires stakeholders to act in the best interest of the child.

The moral and psychological components of criminal responsibility are factors in defining a juvenile, with the primary objectives being the promotion of the juvenile's well-being and the principle of proportionality.
